publish.title: The padlock in your browser, explained
publish.description: What HTTPS and the padlock actually tell you, and what they do not.

scenes.headline: The padlock, explained
scenes.narration: That small padlock in your address bar does one specific job. Here is what it means, and what it does not.

scenes.headline: HTTPS encrypts the trip
scenes.narration: HTTPS is the web's normal protocol with encryption added. It stops anyone between you and the site from reading or changing what you send.

scenes.headline: What happens when you connect
scenes.narration: Your browser asks the site for a secure connection. The site presents a certificate, the two agree on secret keys, and from then on everything is encrypted.
items: Your browser asks for a secure connection

scenes.headline: Who vouches for a site
scenes.narration: A certificate authority is an organisation that signs digital certificates. Your browser trusts a list of them, so a signed certificate lets it verify a site's identity.

definition.meaning: An organisation that signs digital certificates, so browsers can verify a site's identity.

scenes.headline: The padlock is not a verdict
scenes.narration: The padlock means the connection is encrypted. Chrome's own research found that many people read it as a sign a site is trustworthy, and it is not.

scenes.headline: Read the address first
scenes.narration: Check the address in the bar, not just the padlock, before you type a password.
